title: Module Overview: Alternating Block Sum Divisibility
content: The docstring sets up the central theme: when a base $b$ satisfies $b \equiv -1 \pmod{d}$, divisibility by $d$ can be tested by computing an alternating sum of digit blocks in base $b$. The canonical examples are $10 \equiv -1 \pmod{11}$ (single-digit alternating sum) and $1000 \equiv -1 \pmod{7}$ (3-digit block alternating sum). This file provides the general principle and four concrete instantiations.
mathContext: If $b^k \equiv -1 \pmod{d}$, then $n = \sum_i a_i (b^k)^i \equiv \sum_i (-1)^i a_i \pmod{d}$, where each $a_i$ is a $k$-digit block. The alternating sum $a_0 - a_1 + a_2 - \cdots$ is divisible by $d$ iff $n$ is.

title: The Key Congruence: 1000 ≡ −1 (mod 7)
content: The fact $1000 \bmod 7 = 6$ is the arithmetic foundation for the 3-digit block rule for 7. Since $6 = 7 - 1 \equiv -1 \pmod{7}$, successive powers of 1000 alternate sign modulo 7: $1000^0 \equiv 1$, $1000^1 \equiv -1$, $1000^2 \equiv 1$, etc. The proof uses `native_decide`, which evaluates the modular arithmetic at compile time. This is a classic 'numerical coincidence' — 1001 = 7 × 11 × 13 — that makes 3-digit blocks work for both 7 and 13.

title: Congruence Transfer: n ≡ altDigitSum₁₀₀₀(n) (mod 7)
content: seven_modEq_altDigitSum_1000 instantiates the parent module's general `modEq_alternating_digits_sum` with $d = 7$, $b = 1000$. The proof is a one-liner: supply the positivity proof `(by norm_num)` and the key congruence `thousand_mod_seven`. This demonstrates the power of the abstraction in DivisibilityRules.lean — once the general theorem is proved, each new instance is trivial.
mathContext: $n \equiv \text{altDigitSum}_{1000}(n) \pmod{7}$, where $\text{altDigitSum}_{1000}(n) = a_0 - a_1 + a_2 - \cdots$ and $n = a_0 + a_1 \cdot 1000 + a_2 \cdot 1000^2 + \cdots$

title: General Alternating Block Rule: dvd_iff_dvd_altDigitSum
content: This is the central theorem of the file. Given any $d > 0$ and base $b$ with $b \equiv -1 \pmod{d}$, we have $d \mid n \iff d \mid \text{altDigitSum}_b(n)$. The proof converts the congruence $n \equiv \text{altDigitSum}_b(n) \pmod{d}$ (from the parent module) into a biconditional divisibility statement. Each direction uses the same pattern: $d \mid (n - \text{alt})$ and $d \mid \text{alt}$ together imply $d \mid n$ (and vice versa), via `dvd_add` and `sub_add_cancel`. This unifies all alternating-sum divisibility rules under a single framework.
mathContext: For $d > 0$ and $b \bmod d = d - 1$: $d \mid n \iff d \mid \text{altDigitSum}_b(n)$. Proof sketch: $n - \text{alt} \equiv 0 \pmod{d}$, so $d \mid n \iff d \mid \text{alt}$.

title: Instantiation: Divisibility by 7 via 3-Digit Blocks
content: seven_dvd_iff_altDigitSum is the headline result: $7 \mid n$ iff $7$ divides the alternating sum of the 3-digit blocks of $n$. The proof is a direct application of the general rule with the precomputed congruence. This is a practical divisibility test: for 1234567, the blocks are [567, 234, 1] and the alternating sum is 567 − 234 + 1 = 334, which is not divisible by 7, confirming 7 ∤ 1234567.
mathContext: $7 \mid n \iff 7 \mid (a_0 - a_1 + a_2 - \cdots)$ where $n = a_0 + a_1 \cdot 1000 + a_2 \cdot 1000^2 + \cdots$ and each $a_i \in \{0, \ldots, 999\}$.

title: Divisibility by 13: Same 3-Digit Block Trick
content: Because $1000 = 76 \times 13 + 12$ and $12 = 13 - 1$, the same 3-digit block alternating sum that tests divisibility by 7 also tests divisibility by 13. This is not a coincidence — it follows from $1001 = 7 \times 11 \times 13$, so $1000 \equiv -1$ modulo each of 7, 11, and 13. The three theorems (thousand_mod_thirteen, thirteen_modEq_altDigitSum_1000, thirteen_dvd_iff_altDigitSum) mirror the structure for 7 exactly.
mathContext: $1000 \bmod 13 = 12 = 13 - 1$, so $1000 \equiv -1 \pmod{13}$. Therefore $13 \mid n \iff 13 \mid \text{altDigitSum}_{1000}(n)$. The factorization $1001 = 7 \times 11 \times 13$ explains why 3-digit blocks work for all three primes.

title: Concrete Verification Examples
content: Four `example` declarations verify the rules on concrete numbers using `native_decide` and `norm_num`. The example $7 \mid 1001$ is particularly illuminating: in base 1000, $1001 = [1, 1]$, so the alternating sum is $1 - 1 = 0$, and $7 \mid 0$. The example $91 = 7 \times 13$ shows a number divisible by both 7 and 13, connecting to the shared block structure. These are not just tests — they serve as documentation, demonstrating how the abstract rule applies in practice.

title: Classical Instances: Divisibility by 11 and 101
content: These two theorems show the general framework recovering well-known rules. For 11: since $10 \equiv -1 \pmod{11}$, the alternating sum of single digits tests divisibility by 11 — the classical rule taught in school. For 101: since $100 \equiv -1 \pmod{101}$, alternating 2-digit blocks work. Both proofs are one-liners applying `dvd_iff_dvd_altDigitSum` with `native_decide` for the congruence. This demonstrates that the general principle subsumes all known alternating-sum divisibility rules.
mathContext: $11$: $10 \equiv -1 \pmod{11}$, so $11 \mid n \iff 11 \mid (d_0 - d_1 + d_2 - \cdots)$ for decimal digits $d_i$. $101$: $100 \equiv -1 \pmod{101}$, so $101 \mid n \iff 101 \mid (b_0 - b_1 + b_2 - \cdots)$ for 2-digit blocks $b_i$.

title: Summary: Seven Theorems, Zero Axioms
content: The closing summary catalogues all proved results: 5 main theorems (the general rule plus instantiations for 7, 13, 11, and 101) and 2 modular congruence lemmas. The entire development is axiom-free and sorry-free, relying on the `modEq_alternating_digits_sum` infrastructure from the parent module. The key mathematical insight — that $1001 = 7 \times 11 \times 13$ gives simultaneous alternating-sum rules for three primes — unifies what might otherwise seem like separate tricks.
mathContext: The factorization $1001 = 7 \times 11 \times 13$ means $1000 \equiv -1 \pmod{p}$ for $p \in \{7, 11, 13\}$, giving simultaneous 3-digit block rules. Combined with $10 \equiv -1 \pmod{11}$ and $100 \equiv -1 \pmod{101}$, this covers all standard alternating-sum divisibility tests.
